sections.title: UB discipline — where C++ punishes the unwary

blocks.label: traps and their fixes
blocks.py:
# TRAP 1: integer division floor toward NEGATIVE infinity
-7 // 2 == -4            # C++ gives -3! Know the difference
mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2

# TRAP 2: no fixed-width overflow - ints are arbitrary precision
big = 10**30 * 10**30    # fine. Modulo discipline still used for speed.

# TRAP 3: shifting
1 << 31                  # perfectly legal - no sign-bit UB in Python

# TRAP 4: float equality
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3         # False! use math.isclose for floats

blocks.text: Strict weak ordering — the silent killer

# comparator contract becomes a KEY function (always well-ordered):
words.sort(key=lambda w: (len(w), w))   # length asc, ties alphabetical

# multi-key descending on one field:
items.sort(key=lambda p: (-p.score, p.id))

# functools.cmp_to_key exists for true comparators - avoid when possible.

blocks.md: Answers demanded modulo 10⁹+7 (prime) exist to fit in 64 bits while keeping numbers huge. Rules: add/subtract freely with %; MULTIPLY ONLY AFTER widening; division becomes modular inverse via Fermat: `a^(M−2)`.

blocks.label: the three tools
blocks.py:
MOD = 10**9 + 7

def modmul(a, b): return (a % MOD) * (b % MOD) % MOD

def modpow(base, exp):            # built-in: pow(base, exp, MOD)
    r = 1; base %= MOD
    while exp > 0:
        if exp & 1: r = r * base % MOD
        base = base * base % MOD
        exp >>= 1
    return r

def moddiv(a, b): return a * modpow(b, MOD - 2) % MOD   # Fermat inverse

blocks.title: Trace: modpow(3, 13, MOD) — consuming exponent bits

blocks.md: **Negative modulo trap:** `(a−b) % MOD` can print negative in C++. Canonical fix: `((a − b) % MOD + MOD) % MOD`.

items.q: MOD must be prime for Fermat inverse because…
options: a^(p−2) identity requires gcd(a,p)=1 guaranteed by primality
items.explain: Composite modulus needs extended-Euclid inverse instead.

items.q: Counting paths under grid mod 1e9+7: intermediate sums may reach…
items.explain: One multiply doubles digit count; one add doesn't. Widen exactly at multiplies.

sections.title: CP problem set — foundations-tier machinery drills

items.title: Fast-IO Scaffold + Type Discipline Warmup
items.statement: Read t, then t lines of two integers up to 10¹⁸ each; output their product mod 1e9+7. Must pass 10⁶-line input in <1s.
hints: Stress locally with generator script before submitting.

solutionCode.label: IO preamble + every product through modmul
solutionCode.py:
MOD = 1_000_000_007


def modmul(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return ((a % MOD) * (b % MOD)) % MOD


def main() -> None:
    import sys
    data = sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()   # one syscall, not one per line
    t = int(data[0])
    out = []
    for i in range(t):
        a, b = int(data[1 + 2 * i]), int(data[2 + 2 * i])
        out.append(modmul(a, b))
    sys.stdout.write("\n".join(map(str, out)) + "\n")

items.complexity: O(t) with O(1) per line. The win is constant-factor: untied cin/cout handles 10^6 lines well under 1s, where endl-flushed iostream does not.

followups.q: Do the overflow arithmetic out loud.
followups.a: Inputs reach 10^18, which fits in a signed 64-bit int (max ≈ 9.2×10^18) but their product does not. Reducing each operand mod 10^9+7 first bounds both below 2^30, so the product is below 2^60 — safely inside 64 bits. Reduce before multiplying, never after.

followups.q: Why does endl cost so much?
followups.a: endl writes a newline *and* flushes the stream. At 10^6 lines that is 10^6 flushes, each a syscall. Writing '\n' lets the buffer fill and flush in large blocks. Combined with sync_with_stdio(false), this is usually the difference between TLE and comfortable.

items.title: Optimised Sieve + Complexity Defense
items.statement: Implement sieve to 10⁷ with bitset/vector<bool>; defend O(n log log n) using harmonic-style sum n/2+n/3+n/5+… and memory math (bytes used).
hints: Sum over primes p≤n of n/p = n·ln ln n.
vector<bool>: 1 bit per entry — say why byte-array variant trades speed/space.
Odd-only sieve halves memory — implement as extension.

solutionCode.label: odd-only sieve: half the memory, half the marking
solutionCode.py:
def sieve_odd_only(n: int) -> list[int]:
    """Indexes ODD numbers only: index i represents the value 2*i + 1."""
    primes = [2] if n >= 2 else []
    if n < 3:
        return primes
    size = (n - 1) // 2                     # odd values 3,5,7,... up to n
    comp = bytearray(size + 1)
    i = 1
    while 2 * i + 1 <= int(n ** 0.5):
        if not comp[i]:
            p = 2 * i + 1
            # first multiple with no smaller factor is p*p, and p*p is odd
            for j in range(p * p, n + 1, 2 * p):   # step 2p stays on odd multiples
                comp[(j - 1) // 2] = 1
        i += 1
    primes.extend(2 * i + 1 for i in range(1, size + 1) if not comp[i])
    return primes

items.complexity: Time O(n log log n). Memory: vector<bool> at 10^7 is ~1.25 MB (1 bit each); a byte array would be 10 MB. The odd-only variant halves the bit count again to ~625 KB.

followups.a: For each prime p ≤ n the inner loop runs about n/p times, so total work is n·Σ(1/p) over primes p ≤ n. Mertens’ theorem gives Σ(1/p) ≈ ln ln n, so the sum is n·ln ln n. The key point is that it sums over *primes*, not all integers — summing 1/k over every k would give the harmonic series and O(n log n).

followups.q: Why step by 2p instead of p?
followups.a: p is odd, so p·p is odd. Adding p once lands on an even multiple, which the odd-only array does not represent at all. Stepping 2p skips straight to the next odd multiple — which is also why this variant halves the marking work, not just the memory.

items.title: Product of Primes in [L,R] mod M
items.statement: Compose segmented sieve + empty-product edge cases + modmul chain across the window.
hints: Zero primes in window → answer 1? Clarify statement semantics first.
Window scan multiplies through modmul only.

solutionCode.label: segmented sieve, then a modmul chain over the window

items.complexity: Time O((R−L+1) log log R + √R). Space O(√R + (R−L+1)).

followups.q: What should an empty window return, and why clarify it first?
followups.a: The empty product is 1 by convention — it is the multiplicative identity, the same reason 0! = 1. But some statements want 0 for "no primes found". This is genuinely ambiguous, so ask before coding; picking silently is how you fail a test you never saw.

followups.q: Why write `1 % M` instead of just 1?
followups.a: When M = 1 every residue is 0, and a bare 1 would be an out-of-range answer. `1 % M` normalises the identity into the ring. The explicit M == 1 early return makes it obvious, but the habit matters when M is a parameter.

items.title: Modular Exponentiation (iterative, battle-safe)
items.statement: Compute (a^b) % M for b up to 10¹⁸; handle a=0, M=1, negative a normalization.
hints: Reduce a % M first including negatives: ((a%M)+M)%M.
Trace exponent bits on paper for b=13 before coding.

solutionCode.label: square-and-multiply with defensive normalisation

items.complexity: Time O(log b) — about 60 iterations for b up to 10^18. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why the double modulo in `((a % M) + M) % M`?
followups.a: In C++ (and Python for the first step here) a negative dividend can yield a negative remainder — (-7) % 3 is -1 in C++. Adding M lifts it into range, and the second % handles the case where a was already non-negative and the addition overshot. It is the standard normalisation idiom.

followups.q: What is a^0 and 0^0 under this code?
followups.a: The loop never runs for b = 0, so it returns 1 % M — including for a = 0. Defining 0^0 = 1 is the standard convention in modular arithmetic and combinatorics; flag it as an assumption rather than letting the judge decide for you.

items.title: SPOJ EKO — Binary Search on Answer (preview)
items.statement: Max height H so that cutting trees yields ≥ M wood. Monotonic feasibility ⇒ binary search the ANSWER space, not an array.
hints: Feasible(H) is monotone: taller cut ⇒ less wood.
This pattern returns in Module 04 with Aggressive Cows & Book Allocation.

solutionCode.label: binary search the ANSWER, not the array

items.complexity: Time O(n log(maxHeight)) — a linear feasibility check inside a binary search over the answer range. Space O(1).

followups.q: What makes the answer space binary-searchable?
followups.a: Feasible(h) — "cutting at h yields at least M wood" — is monotone: raising the saw never increases the harvest. So the predicate is a run of trues followed by a run of falses, and you are looking for the last true. Monotonicity is the entire licence to binary search; without it the technique is invalid.

With heights up to 10^9 and a sum up to 10^18, lo + hi can overflow a 32-bit int and, in the general case, even approach the 64-bit ceiling. The subtraction form never exceeds the larger operand. It costs nothing and removes an entire class of bug.

items.title: Comparator Contract Autopsy
items.statement: Given a broken `<=` comparator crashing sort on duplicates, prove violation, fix it, write the 3-rule strict-weak-ordering checklist from memory.
hints: Test suite MUST include equal elements — that's what detonates it.
Explain how libstdc++ descends out-of-bounds when contract breaks.

solutionCode.label: the broken comparator, the fix, and the three rules

items.complexity: Not a complexity problem. A comparator that violates strict weak ordering makes std::sort read out of bounds — undefined behaviour, typically a segfault on inputs containing duplicates.

followups.q: Why does a test suite without duplicates fail to catch this?
followups.a: With all-distinct elements, `a <= b` and `a < b` agree on every pair, so the broken comparator behaves perfectly. The violation is only observable when a == b, where `<=` returns true and claims an element precedes itself. Duplicates are the detonator — a test set without them proves nothing.

followups.q: Why is it a crash rather than merely a wrong order?
followups.a: std::sort trusts the comparator as a loop bound. In partitioning it advances a pointer while `cmp(*p, pivot)` holds; with `<=`, an element equal to the pivot never terminates the scan, so the pointer walks off the end of the array. The contract is not a style guide — the library’s memory safety depends on it.

revisionCard: Read CONSTRAINTS first — they select the algorithm class
Preamble: sync off · tie null · '\n' not endl · ll by default
Overflow: widen BEFORE multiply (1LL*a*b) · mid = lo+(hi-lo)/2 · 1<<31 is UB
Comparator = strict weak ordering or sort corrupts memory; test with equal keys
Iterator invalidation: vector reallocates→all die; list/map/set never
Mod world: widen at multiplies only · ((a-b)%M+M)%M · inverse via a^(M-2) (prime M)

glossary.def: Mapping from input bound to affordable complexity (~10⁸ ops/sec heuristic).
Irreflexive, asymmetric, transitive comparison contract required by sort/set/map.
Rules determining which iterators/references survive container mutation.
b^(M−2) mod prime M playing the role of 1/b under mod arithmetic.
Σn style limits bounding TOTAL input across test cases.
Searching monotonic feasible/infeasible boundary over values instead of array positions.
Standard imposes no requirements — compiler may assume impossibility and misoptimize.
